lesson.title: What Comes Back Out: Understanding Output
lesson.summary: An output is the result a function produces after applying its rule to a chosen input, the paired value that makes a function's behavior visible.
lesson.body:
If an input is what you feed into a function, the output is what comes back out after the function's rule has been applied. Continuing the machine analogy, once an input drops into the machine's slot and the machine processes it according to its rule, whatever emerges from the other side is the output. In an ordered pair like (3, 7) belonging to a function, the output is always the second number, 7, the result that was produced once the input, 3, was run through the function.

Outputs live in the range of the function, the complete set of values the function can actually produce, a concept you have already studied closely. Every output that comes out of a function belongs to its range by definition; the range is essentially the list of every possible output collected together. Because a function guarantees exactly one output per input, you never have to wonder which output goes with which input, there is only ever one correct answer once the input and the rule are both known.

Return to the function f(x) = 3x - 2 used earlier. When the input was 4, the output was calculated as f(4) = 3(4) - 2 = 12 - 2 = 10, so 10 is the output paired with the input 4, giving the ordered pair (4, 10). When the input was -1, the output was f(-1) = 3(-1) - 2 = -3 - 2 = -5, giving the ordered pair (-1, -5). In both cases, the output is the number that results after the input has been multiplied by 3 and then had 2 subtracted from it, the specific rule that this particular function follows.

It helps to notice that different inputs can sometimes land on the same output, even though a function never allows the reverse. Consider f(x) = x^2. The input 3 produces the output f(3) = 3^2 = 9. The input -3 produces the output f(-3) = (-3)^2 = 9 as well. Two different inputs, 3 and -3, both produced the identical output, 9. This is completely permitted, since the rule that is forbidden is one input producing two different outputs, not two inputs producing the same output. If you organize a table of values for f(x) = x^2, you will see this pattern repeat: the outputs for 1 and -1 both land on 1, the outputs for 2 and -2 both land on 4, and so on, a mirror-image pattern that comes directly from squaring.

Because the output's value is entirely determined by whichever input was chosen and the function's rule, the output is often called the dependent variable, a term covered next in this unit: dependent because its value depends entirely on the input, it cannot be picked freely the way an input can. Once you can reliably identify an input, apply a function's rule to it, and correctly report the resulting output, you already have the core mechanical skill that function notation and evaluating functions will simply organize into a cleaner, more efficient form of writing. In a table of values, the output column is always filled in after the input column, since every output is calculated from an input rather than chosen on its own, and getting that order right, input first, then output, is worth treating as a fixed habit rather than a guess made problem by problem.
